This paper discusses the development of multiple autonomous navigation strategies for robots in complex, dynamic environments, specifically focusing on a stratified approach. Initially, we outline the principles behind three key navigation algorithms: velocity obstacles, elastic potential fields, and TEB (Timed Elastic Band) controllers. Subsequently, we detail the implementation of real-time navigation using sonar sensors and a ROS-based architecture. Finally, we outline the results obtained from testing the elastic potential fields and stratified controllers in a real-world setting.

Deepfakes and artificial intelligence-generated content are escalating the production of deceptive news, which poses a significant risk to society. To address this issue, researchers are working on developing efficient methods for detecting false news. A prevalent approach involves employing deep learning models to classify news articles as true or false based on their content. However, this approach is hampered by the scarcity of labeled data. To overcome this challenge, we explore a two-stage pipeline that utilizes reassembly-based text simplification to generate altered versions of both true and false news articles. This technique generates altered articles that retain the same meaning as the original, allowing for a more effective and distinguishable learning process in a downstream deep learning model for news verification. Experimental results on the PolitiFact dataset show a significant improvement in accuracy, with a 0.05 increase in F1-score compared to a baseline model trained on the same data.

A fundamental issue in geostatistics and spatial statistics involves modeling data on curved surfaces, which can be considered as a subset of more general manifolds. This research focuses on developing and examining the properties of stationary and non-stationary stochastic models, specifically the minimal surface model and the Laplace-Helmholtz model, within the context of flat domains. Theoretical proofs are provided to demonstrate the positive definiteness of the corresponding spectral densities for both stochastic models. Furthermore, numerical simulations are conducted to illustrate the behavior of the covariance functions of these models.

We develop an efficient algorithm for identifying a low-rank approximation in data that adheres to a norm, specifically for rotationally symmetric data. Our approach begins by mathematically defining a class of norms that are rotatorily symmetric and identifying their corresponding dual norms. Our analysis of this class reveals that the norms they represent are rotationally symmetric and that their dual norms are convex and star-shaped with respect to a unit sphere. Our proposed algorithm for low norm approximation iterates in steps that are bounded and proportional to the complexity of the data divided by its dimension. Our method also allows for the extraction of the underlying structure of data that is elliptical in shape. Our work contributes to the understanding of how norms that are rotationally symmetric can be used to identify and evaluate the importance of data components.

Semantic tagging using deep learning has been widely applied in various areas, including content-based filtering, information retrieval, and question answering. However, existing deep learning-based semantic tagging methods do not account for the impact of a user's intent on the performance of the models. In the case of textual inputs with a high emotional intensity, current deep learning methods may not perform as effectively as they do for low-emotion performance. This study proposes a method that adjusts the performance of a semantic tagging model specifically for textual inputs with a high emotional intensity, in order to enhance the performance of emnona in the field of question answering. The results of the study show that the proposed method can significantly improve the performance of the baseline model, with an increase of 10.4% in F1-score and 10.1% in accuracy.

This paper introduces HiTMap, an innovative approach to representing and navigating unfamiliar environments. Unlike current methods, HiTMap addresses the scalability limitations of topological diagram representations by employing a hierarchical structure. This design divides the environment into multiple sub-regions, each with its own representation, linked together based on connectivity. Furthermore, HiTMap leverages a factor graph-based learning method to automatically extract features from raw sensor data, eliminating the need for manual annotation. To handle large environments, HiTMap also incorporates a strategy for selecting the most relevant sub-region representations. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap in navigating unfamiliar environments.

Employing atomic interferometry, we can accurately measure minute changes in local magnetic fields. To demonstrate this, we successfully detected and quantified the repulsive magnetic fields generated when light shines on a superconductor exhibiting the Meissner effect. Utilizing a 10 cm diameter niobium disk, our measurements were precise enough to detect these magnetic fields with minimal uncertainty. Our atomic sensor exhibited exceptional sensitivity, capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields. Our detection method's high spatial resolution allowed us to map the Meissner effect's characteristics at a fine scale. Our setup's large detection area and compact size make it suitable for monitoring complex magnetic fields in various applications, including quantum computing systems.

This presentation delves into the fundamental properties of finite mixture models, drawing a connection with stochastic geometry. Initially, we examine the representation of a probability distribution as a combination of other distributions, a concept that serves as the basis for models like Gaussian Mixture Models. A key challenge in this area is determining whether one distribution can be represented as a combination of another, a problem that has two distinct sub-problems depending on the number of distributions used in the combination. A stochastic geometry approach to this problem is presented, along with a discussion of the connection between mixture models and the deconvolution process. A notable property of mixtures is their robustness, a concept that is explored in depth. A connection is also drawn between mixtures and the positive part of a function, a concept that is explained in the context of machine learning. Finally, we discuss the connection between mixtures and the Choquet integral, a concept that is explained in depth.

High-performance graphics processing relies heavily on the speed of memory access, yet conventional memory allocators in programming languages like C++ often fail to take full advantage of the available GPU memory due to their sequential nature. This limitation becomes especially apparent when working with large datasets that exceed the capacity of high-end GPUs. In this work, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator designed to leverage the parallel processing capabilities of GPUs. DynaSOAr employs a bank-based approach to memory allocation, allowing it to efficiently manage large-scale object-oriented programs. Our allocator features automatic scheduling and a cache-oblivious strategy, enabling it to adapt to varying data sizes and access patterns. Experimental results show that DynaSOAr outperforms traditional memory allocators in terms of execution time and can handle datasets up to 10 times larger than the available GPU memory.

The Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state theory, which describes magnetic impurities on superconductors, has traditionally been described using a non-relativistic initial principles approach. However, this method often fails to accurately predict the position of the magnetic state within the superconducting gap due to errors in the spin moment calculation. To address this issue, we have modified the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state theory to incorporate the effects of initial principles theory's effect on orbital moment, a critical factor in determining the magnetic state's position. This updated approach has been used to investigate the magnetic properties of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the surface of superconducting Nb(110). By utilizing a modified Hubbard approach to describe the d-electrons of Mn, we have been able to accurately predict the magnetic state's position within the superconducting gap, a key metric for validating the state theory.

The NASA TOI-712.1 star system was characterized for the first time as a multi-planet system in this study, with the parent star being classified as an early F-type star with a temperature of 6400K and a radius of 1.04 solar radii. Through the combination of data from the TESS mission and the CHEOPS satellite, three confirmed planets and two additional candidates were identified within the system. By applying a power law distribution to the radius measurements of TESS detected exoplanets, the study determined that the probability of the TOI-712 field being filled with planets was 99.9%. The radius migration pattern indicated that the TOI-712 field was likely populated with planets, with TOI-712 b, c, and d being the most probable candidates. The study concluded that TOI-712 d, located in the system's outer region, was the most intriguing exoplanet due to its potential to experience liquid water on its surface, with a radius of 1.98 Earth radii and an orbital period of 200 days.

This study examines the adsorption of carbon and nitrogen atoms onto TiO2-rutile using density functional theory, with a focus on understanding how these atoms affect the material's electronic and magnetic properties. By modeling various configurations of C and N atoms in different surface sites, we determined the most stable arrangements and calculated the energy required to create defects in the material. Our results show that C and N atoms can introduce mid-gap states that could potentially be used to manipulate the material's band gap, with nitrogen atoms being more likely to occur naturally in the material than C atoms. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of the material when infused with specific elements and could have implications for using TiO2-rutile in electronic and magnetic applications.

We propose that the Large Hadron Collider's elastic scattering process can effectively produce top quarks in an elastic-proton fixed target configuration. Due to the preservation of elastic protons in this process, the method benefits from exceptionally high purity, making it an ideal tool for top quark property research. The top quark production potential of this process is particularly pronounced at high energies, with the elastic scattering cross section exceeding 10 picobarns for a 13 TeV proton collision. Furthermore, the method enables access to a unique top quark production region with large momentum transfer, a region inaccessible through conventional proton-proton collision methods. The unique production region allows for the determination of the top quark's electric charge and spin, two properties that are difficult to ascertain through conventional collision methods. The feasibility of this method is supported by Monte Carlo simulations, which indicate that the LHC can produce approximately 10 million top quark pairs and decays per year in this configuration.

A graph's top Ramsey density, denoted as $\text{tr}(\Gamma)$, is defined such that there exists an infinite subgraph within the graph $G$ whose subgraph, $R(H)$, has the property that for any edge-colored version of $G$, either $R(H)$ contains a monochromatic edge-colored subgraph isomorphic to one of the copies of the infinite graph pattern $\Gamma$. In 2018, Fox, Shen, and Zhao established upper and lower bounds for the top density of graph components, showing that for any infinite graph pattern $\Gamma$, the top density $\text{t}(\Gamma)$ and top Ramsey density, $\text{tr}(\Gamma)$, satisfy the inequality $\text{tr}(\Gamma) \leq \text{t}(\Gamma) + 1 \leq 2\text{tr}(\Gamma)$. They also provided specific examples demonstrating that for certain graphs, the top density can be strictly greater than 1. In this work, we further investigate the relationship between the two densities, proving that for any graph, the difference between the two densities is at most 1, and there exist examples where the two densities are not equal.

Our quantum-accurate Qutrit simulations of Schwinger QED in a linearly polarized vacuum have been found to be notably superior to those made with qubits. In our analysis, we found that Qutrits can accurately represent the QED's fundamental particles, photons, due to their inherent properties. In contrast, Qubits in a two-dimensional Hilbert space have been found to be limited to representing either particles or collective excitations, but not both simultaneously. Our findings are derived from a detailed examination of Qutrit and Qubit representations of the asymptotic Fock states in the linearly polarized vacuum.

A theoretical investigation into the behavior of polarized positrons undergoing QED interactions has been conducted, with a focus on how their polarization changes as they decelerate near a metal surface after being accelerated by ultra-intense laser pulses. A comprehensive formula has been derived that describes the average polarization loss experienced by these positrons. A computational model has been developed to apply this formula to a specific scenario, where a positron is exposed to an extremely powerful, linearly polarized laser beam near a metallic surface. This model demonstrates that, under ideal conditions with a specific laser intensity and frequency, a positron will emit approximately 20,000 photons as it interacts with the laser, resulting in a significant decrease in its initial polarization of about 50%. A subsequent analysis has been performed to determine the average polarization loss experienced by a population of positrons moving in the same direction and possessing similar properties. This analysis reveals that, for a population of thick positrons, the average polarization loss is approximately 40%.

We establish that the class of hereditary circular arc graphs can be efficiently broken down into smaller groups, specifically 555-limitied groups of size 2^(O(n)) and O(n^3). Additionally, we demonstrate a method to identify these smaller groups in O(m^0.774 + n) time, building on a recent breakthrough by Woodruff and Zhou. This finding implies a efficient detection algorithm for circular arc properties with input size f(m,n).

A new ultra-low voltage temperature sensor is introduced that operates within a 0.6V to 1.8V supply range. Utilizing a fully integrated design, the circuit exhibits a temperature coefficient of 12.6mV/°C² and maintains a linearity error of 0.24°C across its operating temperature spectrum of -40°C to 125°C. The converter's initial and maximum output errors are 1.4°C, with a supply voltage conversion rate of 100ppm/V, a conversion time of 100μs, a power consumption of 1.06pJ per conversion, and an operational frequency of 1MHz. The device also features a 1.4°C temperature resolution, a 100μs conversion time, and a power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion.

We introduce the concept of Lie groupoid configurations and demonstrate how specific groupoid constructions, such as the pullback along a smooth map and the composition of two Lie groupoids, correspond to functors and natural transformations. Additionally, we establish a connection between geometric configurations on Lie groupoids and the 2-categorical relationships between smooth stacks, showing that Lie groupoids serve as 2-functorial presentations for smooth stacks. We derive key properties, including the characterization of equivalences and calculable limits and colimits, from these properties.

Recent infrared observations of the Dragon Nebula, a prominent infrared dark nebula in the Orion Molecular Cloud, reveal a distinctive hourglass or rugby ball shape. This unique structure is characterized by a central region of increased brightness and density, which may be the precursor to a protostar. The brightness and density of this central region are comparable to those of observed protostellar envelopes, and it exhibits a rotational pattern around an axis perpendicular to the line of sight. These findings suggest that the expansion of a dense core could be the key to the formation of massive stars in dark nebulae.

This research paper establishes conditions for a real-valued, mean-zero, stationary random field to possess specific properties, such as continuous spectra or positive densities, in a single-step framework. It demonstrates that certain conditions, including those derived by Yaglom and Gneiting, are both necessary and sufficient for the existence of such single-step realizations. Furthermore, the paper derives the corresponding two-dimensional results and provides methods to calculate the density in both cases.

We investigate the flow of a liquid foam through a pipe to uncover the underlying mechanisms of its flow resistance. Our study reveals that the pressure loss in pipe pipe radius R and pipe length L. The primary mechanism of resistance is found to be the friction between the pipe wall and the gas film on the surface of the foam bulk. This film's thickness is determined by the balance of surface tension and inertia forces. The film's behavior is described by a scaling law, which is validated experimentally. The film's effective roughness is estimated and used to calculate the friction factor, which is found to be consistent with existing data.

This research focuses on classifying skin lesions into benign and malignant categories using a dataset of 10,000 clinical images. A novel approach is proposed to identify cancerous and non-cancerous skin conditions by combining a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and an outlier detection method. The study also explores the use of a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) to enhance classification accuracy. The proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset and shows improved performance compared to existing techniques.

A liquid-liquid displacement experiment on a rotating platform is used to study the interaction of two immiscible fluids with different viscosities. The setup, known as a Hele-Shaw cell, involves fluids of varying densities and viscosities and allows for an expanded range of dimensionless numbers. This approach is effective for examining the dynamics of a flexible interface between the fluids. In this study, researchers focus on the entrainment of a droplet of the outer fluid within the inner fluid and the formation of protrusions on the interface, specifically fingering patterns. The entry of a droplet is characterized by the formation of a neck that eventually pinches off, and the resulting flexible finger can undergo complex deformations, including stretching, coiling, and stretching again. The outcome is influenced by the interplay of forces acting on the interface, and the study provides detailed observations and visual evidence of these phenomena.

Astronomical observations of molecules with cyclic structures have been limited to a small group of species, mainly consisting of linear molecules Cn and CN. A study focusing on spectral data from TMC-1 revealed the presence of two ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers, pre-cumene, and provided a more precise measurement of the pre-cumene to CCH ratio. This discovery of the most complex cyclic molecule in the interstellar medium and an updated assessment of Cn and CN molecule abundances within this type of environment marks significant advancements in our understanding of cyclic molecule formation in the interstellar medium.

and at each step, the next symbol is predicted based on previously predicted
symbols and input text. In this paper, we introduce a new method, Look-ahead
Focus, to enhance the model by incorporating the relationship between prior
content and the upcoming text. Specifically, we divide the preceding content
into relevant and irrelevant parts, predict symbols for the relevant part
character-by-character, and perform attention pooling on the irrelevant part
to guide the encoding of the current symbol. We also explore multiple

accuracy and achieves a 2.4x to 4.4x speedup in training. Additionally, we
achieve the highest indentation and variable naming suggestions in the Indent

In 1995, Jeffrey Bradshaw, Gene A. Fox, and Gene Esposito introduced a framework for high-performance computing that incorporated the World Wide Web. Their approach combined elements of object-oriented design and client-server architecture, establishing a prototype for web-based computing frameworks. This paper examines how their framework influenced the development of grid computing, highlighting a key challenge faced by high-performance computing in adapting to everyday users. We argue that grid computing was a significant step forward in addressing this challenge. However, its reliance on a single, monolithic system hindered its long-term effectiveness. We propose that a more adaptable approach, which we term post-grid computing, offers a promising path forward for high-performance computing.

A new combined dark energy and dark matter model, incorporating non-negligible interaction and both dissipative effects, is proposed. A general relativity framework is used to derive the field equations, which are then solved to obtain a solution for a specific anisotropic solution within the combined dark energy and dark matter model. The resulting solution is used to calculate the energy density and pressure, and the rate of entropy change is determined. The solution is then examined in the context of the Holographic Principle, GH bound, and Coboundary bound to ensure its physical consistency. A relationship is established between the solution and the combined dark energy and dark matter, and the solution is found to be consistent with observations. The solution is also used to calculate the equation of state, and the solution is found to be in the dark matter regime. The solution is also used to calculate the sound speed, and the solution is found to be in the stable regime. The solution is also used to calculate the deceleration parameter, and the solution is found to be in the accelerating regime. The solution is also used to calculate the statefinder parameter, and the solution is found to be in the $\Lambda$CDM regime. Our research investigates the implications of the unexplained missing decay rate of $J/\psi$ particles, with a focus on efficient field theories of neutrinos and dark energy. By applying a quadratic Neumann field theory for neutrinos, we determined the average missing decay rate of $J/\psi$ particles to be approximately $10^{-5}$ times the total decay rate, which is in agreement with experimental data. We also considered two scalar field theories of dark energy, both of which resulted in non-gravitational missing $J/\psi$ decay rates exceeding the observed values. Consequently, our findings suggest that efficient field theories of dark matter and dark energy must be constrained or ruled out, with significant implications for their potential contributions to missing energy in particle decay processes.

This work focuses on a multivariate functional singular spectrum transform (MFSTT) with a detailed examination of its fundamental properties and practical applications. The MFSTT is an advanced technique that builds upon the singular spectrum analysis and functional singular spectrum transform methods, offering a robust tool for dimensionality reduction and pattern recognition in high-dimensional data. The MFSTT's efficacy is demonstrated through theoretical examples, including curve classification and surface recognition, as well as real-world datasets, such as hydroelectric power generation and financial time series. A comprehensive performance evaluation is conducted through statistical hypothesis testing, revealing the MFSTT's superior accuracy compared to traditional dimensionality reduction techniques, such as functional principal component analysis and multivariate singular spectrum transform.

A primary objective in our research is to establish the global persistence of the walk's confinement between barriers for an arbitrary number of barriers and in scenarios with varying distances. Additionally, we examine the impact of asymmetric barriers on the walk and demonstrate the global persistence of its confinement. Our findings reveal that the durations of localization between asymmetric barriers follow a log-normal distribution, and as the barriers become more symmetric, the duration between them exhibits persistence. The concepts of global persistence and its relationship to local persistence are explained in our paper.

The microscopic examination of tissue samples is a key diagnostic tool in cancer detection, and identifying individual cells within microscopic images is a vital task. However, the small size and irregular shapes of cells make this task challenging. In this study, we introduce a new dataset comprising 10,000 microscopic images of tissue from oral cancer patients, and present a new approach for detecting and locating cells in these images. Our method employs a two-step process, where a convolutional network is used to segment cells in the images, and another network is trained to predict cell contours. This approach outperforms existing methods in terms of detection accuracy, and our results are available for public use.

We establish the converse theorem within the context of the odd special orthogonal and symplectic local fields, focusing on a specific range of representations with a reduced dimensionality, over the odd orthogonal and symplectic spaces of a definitive dimensional requirement, all enduring over a non-zero positive characteristic.

We introduce a novel perspective on graph convolutional neural networks (GNNs) by reinterpreting the first layer of GCNs through the lens of matched filtering, which provides a clear and concise proof of the positive semi-definiteness of the GCN kernel. Building on this foundation, we develop a straightforward optimization approach to address the issue of GCN overfitting by limiting the parameters to a positive semi-definite form. Leveraging this insight, we create a new GCN variant called the Matched Filtering GCN (MFGCN), which incorporates the benefits of the original GCN framework while addressing its limitations. Furthermore, we extend the positive semi-definiteness constraint to other commonly used GNN architectures, resulting in enhanced variants of GAT, GraphSAGE, and KGAT. Experimental evaluations on both node and graph classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that MFGCN and its derivative architectures consistently outperform their traditional counterparts across multiple datasets.

We derive an effective action for a single field in three dimensions, consisting of a positive scalar and an $SO(2,1)$-symmetric gravity, by integrating out the CS gauge field. This approach allows us to analyze Einstein-Cartan theory in the context of a complex scalar field, and we demonstrate that the resulting theory matches the conformal gravity with a scalar field when the torsion is treated as a perturbation. This equivalence holds true when the scalar field is massless. However, in cases where the scalar acquires mass, the theory diverges significantly. We then apply this effective action to investigate the thermodynamic and stability properties of a class of exact solutions, including charged spinning solitons and black holes, and we calculate their corrections to mass, horizon radius, and specific heat, all as functions of the mass parameter.

Precise measurement of shear wave velocity is essential in ultrasound elastography, yet it is hindered by the limited spatial resolution of conventional ultrasound imaging. Researchers have developed high-resolution elastography techniques using externally applied pressure patterns, but these require subjects to be exposed to high-intensity ultrasound, which carries potential risks. A novel approach called Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VO-SA) is proposed, combining low-resolution tracking waves and high-resolution reconstructed shear waves to achieve precise wave velocity estimation without compromising safety. VO-SA utilizes multiple transducer transmissions to enhance the resolution of a specific region of interest, enabling precise shear wave velocity estimation through time-of-flight methods. The VO-SA approach was evaluated using both simulated and real ultrasound data, revealing its ability to accurately match the ground truth and conventional methods while providing a 1.7 times improvement in resolution. The proposed method's reliability was further confirmed by comparing its results to those obtained using a known phantom with a shear wave velocity of 3.0 m/s. The VO-SA approach demonstrates its potential to provide precise and safe elastography imaging.

We introduce a novel framework called Rational Pseudocode, which connects traditional algorithm descriptions with behavioral demonstrations. This framework allows for the incorporation of natural language explanations, enabling models to effectively learn complex procedures like dynamic programming and various types of pseudocode. Our approach has been successfully applied to simple and intricate algorithms, yielding models that exhibit accurate behavior in retrieving information from large databases, with a retrieval accuracy of 99.9%. Our code and trained models are available for public use at https://github.com/davidduong/rational-pseudocode.

In numerous practical scenarios, we need to organize large volumes of high-dimensional data into groups based on key characteristics. When new data points are continuously added, traditional group organization methods become inefficient and require significant computational resources. To address this challenge, we developed a dynamic multi-way partitioning algorithm that achieves near-optimal performance, with computational requirements directly proportional to the square root of the product of the number of dimensions, partition count, and data point size. This breakthrough enables efficient management of growing datasets, exemplified by its application in categorizing thousands of genetic markers into partitions for enhanced diagnostic capabilities.

This research focuses on a new way to break down a class of dynamic, probabilistic games played in different environments, specifically the stochastic pursuit-withdrawal games on line and ring networks. A novel hierarchical framework is proposed to analyze these games, consisting of three distinct levels. Initially, a withdrawal point's probabilistic movement is approximated as deterministic, allowing for a pursuit-deception game with deterministic withdrawal points to be examined. This examination reveals that such games can be further divided into a set of pursuit-deception subgames, each possessing a dominant strategy profile that leads to a significant withdrawal range. Consequently, a pursuit-withdrawal game can be further simplified to a pursuit-range game, characterized by a withdrawal range and a corresponding set of pursuit-deception subgames. This hierarchical analysis is then leveraged to provide a more in-depth understanding of the deterministic pursuit-withdrawal games, specifically those played on line and ring networks, and to uncover new, previously unknown properties of the stochastic pursuit-withdrawal games.

Theoretical calculations of high-energy muon collisions with protons and heavy ions are being updated to include the full set of electroweak processes, specifically focusing on the production of two vector bosons. While the leading order calculations account for single vector boson emission, the full set requires the inclusion of WW, WZ, and ZZ final states. A new method is proposed to efficiently apply reweighting techniques to these multi-leg processes, enabling the full set to be simulated using a limited number of event samples. This optimization allows the full set of two vector boson final states to be managed with just four event samples, significantly reducing computational costs.

In reinforcement learning, models have been increasingly utilized to expand the range of experiences an agent encounters, thereby accelerating its learning process. Nevertheless, when models are directly integrated into the learning loop, they pose a risk of entrapment in local optima and learning distorted experiences. This research proposes a novel approach to model-based reinforcement learning, in which agents learn and operate in parallel modular systems, effectively isolating the risks of models while capitalizing on their benefits. We conducted multi-task reinforcement learning experiments using this approach, where our results indicate that this systems-level isolation enables agents to achieve superior performance across multiple tasks, even when one of the modular systems encounters a catastrophic failure.

This paper proves a three spheres theorem for functions in Cl_{r,s} that satisfy $\partial^* \partial u = 0$ within a specific range, given three mutually disjoint spheres in R^{r+1,s}. Specifically, if $\Theta_1$, $\Theta_2$, and $\Theta_2$ do not overlap and there exists a continuous path of configurations of spheres connecting them, such that each configuration consists of mutually non-overlapping spheres, then the $L_\infty$ norm of the function $u$ on any point within the region enclosed by the spheres is bounded by the product of the norms of the function on the boundary spheres, weighted by a polynomial factor. This result is then applied to show the uniqueness of solutions to a Dirac-type equation with a compact support, under the condition that the function satisfies $\partial^* \partial v = f$ in a domain $\Omega$.

To address inverse problems, a new variation of the Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN) has been developed, termed the Regularized Conditional GAN (RCGAN). This new approach modifies the CGAN framework by incorporating a regularization term into the generator's loss function, which encourages a more uniform distribution of conditional samples in the image manifold. This uniformity facilitates the capability to recreate specific input data and perform conditioning transfer, thereby allowing for the reconstruction of unobserved parts of data and the combination of different imaging techniques. Through the RCGAN framework, three applications have been successfully demonstrated, including image completion, denoising, and deconvolution using iterative RCGAN (I-RCGAN) training. The effectiveness of I-RCGAN has also been verified through its application to solving the inverse problem in computed tomography (CT).

This article explores the dynamics of a specific fractional-order map, f, defined by the equation $f(x) = rx^{r-1}$, where the parameter $r$ is greater than one. It is shown through analysis that for this function, there is no invariant curve other than the line representing the main axis. A proof for this statement is constructed using an integral that diverges. Furthermore, the article provides evidence that for any number between zero and one, there is at least one point where the $n$-th iteration of the function results in a value of one when raised to a power of one minus that number. The proof for this claim relies on evaluating the integral of the function's derivative in a specific interval. A numerical example is used to illustrate this phenomenon.

A study of the interstellar medium surrounding the bright pulsar B1133+16 in the Milky Way's inner region was conducted by analyzing scintillation data. A one-dimensional model was used to investigate the distribution of ionized gas along the line of sight, taking into account the characteristics of the scintillation pattern. The results revealed that the region contains a significant amount of ionized gas, with an electron density of approximately 0.02 cm^-3, located about 1.5 kpc from the pulsar. The study also compared the findings with previous research on the gas surrounding the center of the galaxy and found that the conditions are similar to those found in previous studies. The scintillation pattern showed a complex structure, with multiple layers of gas affecting the signal from the pulsar. The study found that the gas is likely organized into a toroidal shape, with the pulsar located outside the center of the torus. The study also noted the presence of a dense gas cloud near the center of the galaxy, which may be related to the gas surrounding the center of the galaxy.

To enhance the performance of generative models in audio signal processing tasks, particularly in applications like TTS and voice synthesis, researchers are focusing on adjusting models to handle periodic and non-periodic segments of sound. However, this problem remains largely unexplored. In response, we introduce a novel generative model called the WaveNet-inspired Periodic Autoregressive Network (WaveNet-PRN), which incorporates pitch information to improve performance. This model features two distinct network structures: a WaveNet-inspired network for low-pitch content and a pitch-aware dilated convolution network for periodic components. Experimental evaluations on two datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WaveNet-PRN, showing a 10% reduction in mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC) and a 12% reduction in mean squared error (MSE) compared to WaveNet in the LibriTTS and LJSpeech datasets.

The coherent nerve functor establishes a right adjunction to the bicategorical arrow category, which can be characterized by the presence of a bicategorical mark, or in simpler terms, the presence of a shadow. This is analogous to the presence of an ordinary 1-categorical mark, or 1-comma, which is the condition for a functor to be considered as part of a bicategorical limit. This is similar to the analogous situation in 2-category theory, where the condition for a functor to be part of a 2-categorical limit is the presence of a comma, or an ordinary 2-comma.

Our primary goal is to directly translate audio data into images depicting sound sources in a 2D space, bypassing the need for geographic or environmental context. Our approach involves training a neural network to handle this challenging task using only raw audio recordings and location images. We discovered that pre-training on synthetic data significantly enhances performance, particularly when employing a versatile spatial encoding method. Our model outperforms previous methods in source localization, even when trained without access to geographical or environmental information.

We introduce a novel variant of standard GNNs called the "Lorentzian Graph Neural Network" (L-GNN), which operates under the assumption that the input graph is weighted with positive and negative edge types. Unlike traditional GNNs, L-GNNs utilize the Lorentzian vector space to perform message passing, which yields more discriminative node embeddings than their Euclidean counterparts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of L-GNNs by using them to solve two real-world graph classification tasks, namely molecular property prediction and new drug discovery, achieving improved results in both cases.

We introduce a novel non-extensive delayed growth and devaluation model based on the
Tsallis entropy principle, and apply it to analyze the behavior of delay depreciation. Our findings reveal that in this context, the non-extensive nature of the system leads to an enhancement of the growth rate, whereas time-decay results in a reduction of the depreciation rate. We also demonstrate that time-decay leads to an increase in the system's non-extensiveness, leading to a self-reinforcing effect. We further show that our model leads to an average delay devaluation rate that is lower than the initial rate, and that the system's non-extensiveness plays a significant role in this outcome. We discuss the implications of these findings for financial contexts, and in particular, for the trading of delayed assets.

We also discuss the concept of a harmonic gauge in this heavy gravity context, and how it differs from its traditional meaning. This research involves transitioning Weyl quantization rules from an abstract framework to a Weyl-Wigner representation, where functions are explicitly depicted. By maintaining this specific representation, we derive conditions for canonical equilibrium states for functions under the double stochasticity constraint, specifically for states defined by the D matrix. These conditions are characterized as the D matrix multiplied by a constant shift function, resulting in a state that adheres to the pureness condition. Furthermore, we establish conditions for canonical equilibrium states described by Boltzmann, Gibbs, and von Mises distributions. Additionally, we establish conditions for pureness and canonical equilibrium states for collective functions, specifically those describing many-body systems, under the same constraint.

The concept of negative absolute temperature, which has been mathematically established since the early 20th century, has been experimentally realized for the first time in solid-state spin systems through nuclear adiabatic demagnetization. This phenomenon occurs when temperatures rise in an isolated system with a limited phase space following the removal of heat. Although initially considered a mathematical curiosity, these temperatures are now significant. This note provides a brief examination of the relevance of negative absolute temperatures and their fundamental properties, as well as their practical applications.

We explore the simplest implementation of the scoto-seesaw mechanism within its minimal framework, extending the Standard Model with an additional real singlet scalar and two types of dark sector doublets. One doublet interacts with the Standard Model through the 't Hooft natural operator, while the other remains naturally light. This model accounts for the observed neutrino masses, the dark matter candidate, and the stability of the electroweak vacuum. We derive the necessary conditions for the dark sector doublets to ensure vacuum stability and examine the implications of the neutrino mass matrix's rank on the model's parameter space. We also investigate the interplay between the neutrino mass matrix's rank and the dark matter properties within this framework.

Rational symplectomorphisms present a challenge in defining the quantum homology of symplectic manifolds due to the difficulty in distinguishing closed and non-closed paths within the manifold. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of relative quantum homology, denoted as $QH_\ast(M,f)$, for a symplectic manifold M and an appropriate regular symplectic transformation f. This new definition enables the construction of a quantum homology sequence for a broad class of symplectic transformations, including those that behave like a "drumhead" and a "bowl" under specific conditions. Furthermore, we establish the invariance of relative quantum homology under suitable conditions, demonstrating its robustness as a topological invariant.

The concept of Illness-Aware Image Modification (IAIM) was introduced to address the limitations of current medical imaging enhancement techniques, which often fail to consider the specific illness being treated. IAIM aims to guide the modification of medical images in a way that preserves the specific features of a disease while improving other aspects of the image. To achieve this, an IIAI model was developed that takes into account both the image and the corresponding illness information. A challenge in IIAIM is the scarcity of data that includes both images and explicit illness information. To overcome this, a new dataset called MIM-CXR-Illness was created by combining information from two existing datasets, CXR14 and MIM-CRD. This new dataset contains a total of 58,000 entries, including 21 different illnesses. A baseline model was also established to compare the IIAIM approach. The IIAIM model was then evaluated using this new dataset and outperformed the baseline model in terms of clinical task performance and image quality.

A data visualization tool called ViDaExpert enables users to effectively examine high-dimensional vector data. This tool allows for flexible, non-linear data examination, offering features such as multiple simultaneous scatter plots, customizable node connections, and advanced filtering options. ViDaExpert is designed to be user-friendly, with an intuitive interface that includes drag-and-drop functionality and pre-set templates for common tasks. The tool is built on the popular Vis.js library and is available free of charge for download from GitHub.
